chunks: "Bare-metal programming means writing firmware that runs directly on the microcontroller's hardware with no operating system underneath. My code is the only software on the chip.
It sets up the clocks, configures the peripherals by writing to their registers, and then controls everything itself. The typical structure is this.
On reset, the CPU loads the stack pointer and jumps to the reset handler. Startup code copies initialised data from flash to RAM, zeroes the uninitialised data, and calls main .
In main I initialise the clock, GPIO, timers and so on, then enter an infinite loop.
Time-critical events are handled by interrupt service routines, which set flags or put data in buffers, and the main loop reacts to them.
For multi-step behaviour I use state machines rather than blocking waits.
The advantages are minimal overhead, full control over timing and power, a tiny memory footprint, and simplicity for small projects.

The disadvantages: I have to manage the scheduling myself, long operations can delay everything else in the loop, I write or integrate all the drivers, and as the project grows, the code gets harder to maintain compared with an RTOS with separate tasks.
For a simple sensor node or a motor controller with one tight loop, bare-metal is often the right call."
